title: Wang et al. — Music interventions for pain and distress during childhood vaccination (Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, 2025)
synopsis: This systematic review and meta-analysis included five randomized trials with 306 children undergoing vaccination. Across the included studies, music interventions were associated with lower pain scores (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.24) and distress scores (SMD −0.83, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.54) than routine care.
appraisal: Only five small trials were included, and music type and duration varied. Results concern acute vaccination procedures and should not be generalized to other clinical settings without evidence.

title: Ou et al. — Music during painful procedures in preterm infants (Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, 2024)
synopsis: This review pooled four randomized trials of music during painful procedures in preterm infants. The authors reported lower Premature Infant Pain Profile scores during and after procedures and improved oxygen saturation; peak heart-rate changes were not statistically significant.
appraisal: The evidence base is small, with only four trials and a need for larger prospective studies. Findings are specific to preterm infants and monitored procedural care.

title: Park et al. — Technology-based music interventions for procedural anxiety and pain (Systematic Review, 2024)
synopsis: This systematic review examined 21 randomized trials of technology-delivered music interventions for people undergoing surgery or procedures. Nine studies reported reduced anxiety and seven reported reduced pain. More than half allowed participants to choose music themes; the review could not determine whether outcomes differed by device or software.
appraisal: Studies and interventions varied, making direct comparisons difficult. The review does not establish which app or device is most effective and its search period predates publication.

title: Mas‑Herrero, et al. — A causal role for the prefrontal cortex in music‑induced reward (J. Neuroscience, 2021)
synopsis: This combined TMS + fMRI study probed the causal role of left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) in music‑induced pleasure and motivation. Stimulation of dlPFC produced bidirectional changes in music reward responses and modulated nucleus accumbens activation and fronto‑auditory functional connectivity.
appraisal: Moderate sample size and short experimental sessions; TMS effects are localized and may not map directly onto naturalistic listening or long‑term therapy.

title: Gold, Pearce, et al. — Pleasurable music modulates reinforcement learning (Frontiers in Psychology, 2013)
synopsis: Behavioral experiments showed that listening to pleasurable music can bias reinforcement learning performance in a probabilistic selection task. Effects varied with musical experience, supporting a link between music reward and dopaminergic learning processes.
appraisal: No direct imaging or neurochemical measures — mechanisms are inferred. Short lab sessions reduce ecological validity for therapeutic settings.

title: Bradt & Dileo — Music interventions for preoperative anxiety (Cochrane Review, 2013 update)
synopsis: The Cochrane meta‑analysis pooled 26 randomized trials (N≈2,051) and found a moderate reduction in preoperative anxiety with music listening versus standard care. While heterogeneity existed across studies, the overall effect supports music as a low‑risk anxiolytic adjunct in perioperative settings.
appraisal: Marked heterogeneity (differences in music protocols, timing, measures), and several small trials with unclear or high risk of bias.

title: Palmer, et al. — Brief music intervention reduces preoperative anxiety (J Clin Oncol, 2015)
synopsis: In a pragmatic randomized trial (n≈201) a single 5‑minute patient‑preferred music session (live or recorded) reduced preoperative anxiety vs usual care, with live music also linked to quicker immediate recovery. The trial demonstrates that very brief, preference‑matched music has measurable perioperative benefits.
appraisal: Immediate outcomes only (no long‑term follow‑up); possible expectancy/placebo effects because full blinding is infeasible with live music.

title: Werner, et al. — Sensorimotor synchronization to music reduces pain (PLOS One, 2023)
synopsis: Experimental evidence shows that active sensorimotor synchronization to music (moving in time with music) yields larger pain reductions than passive listening or silence, indicating that embodied music engagement develops distinct analgesic effects beyond auditory exposure.
appraisal: Laboratory induced pain and short outcomes — careful translation is needed for complex chronic or palliative pain populations.

title: Söderlund, et al. — Noise and ADHD: Stochastic resonance in inattentive children (Dev Psychol, 2010)
synopsis: This foundational study demonstrated that children with ADHD actually perform better on cognitive tasks when exposed to moderate auditory noise (white noise at ~80 dB) compared to silence, while typically developing children showed the opposite pattern. The findings support the Moderate Brain Arousal (MBA) model, suggesting that ADHD brains are understimulated at baseline and benefit from external noise to reach optimal arousal for attention.
appraisal: Single session design; used artificial white noise rather than structured music; individual differences in optimal noise levels suggest personalization is critical.

title: Pickens, Khan, & Berlau — White noise as a possible therapeutic option for children with ADHD (Complementary Therapies in Medicine, 2019)
synopsis: This review discusses white noise as a possible nonpharmacological option for children with ADHD. Its conclusions should not be read as proof that noise benefits every child or that white noise is equivalent to music-based interventions.
appraisal: The review does not establish a universal benefit or show that white noise and music interventions have equivalent effects.

title: Kalas — Joint attention responses of children with autism spectrum disorder to simple versus complex music (Journal of Music Therapy, 2012)
synopsis: This study compared joint-attention responses of children with autism spectrum disorder to simple versus complex music. It examines musical complexity in a specific study context and does not establish a universally preferred style or treatment.
appraisal: Results from a single study and context should not be generalized to all autistic children or all music settings.

title: Rauscher, et al. — Mozart Effect: Music and spatial-temporal reasoning (Nature, 1993)
synopsis: The original Mozart Effect study demonstrated temporary improvement in spatial-temporal reasoning after listening to Mozart's Sonata K.448. While subsequent research has moderated initial claims, the study established that structured, complex tonal music can influence cognitive performance. K.448 remains one of the most studied pieces for neurological effects.
appraisal: Effects are temporary (10-15 minutes); overgeneralized in popular media; mechanism debated (arousal vs. specific musical properties).

title: Thaut & Hoemberg — Neurologic Music Therapy Handbook (Oxford, 2014)
synopsis: The foundational textbook for Neurologic Music Therapy (NMT), establishing evidence-based protocols including Rhythmic Auditory Stimulation (RAS) for gait rehabilitation. The text synthesizes decades of research on how rhythmic entrainment engages motor cortex and can support movement rehabilitation, attention training, and cognitive processing in neurological populations.
appraisal: Clinical protocols require trained therapists for optimal outcomes; self-directed use needs careful adaptation.

title: Chaieb, Wilpert, Reber, & Fell — Auditory beat stimulation and its effects on cognition and mood states (Frontiers in Psychiatry, 2015)
synopsis: This review examines auditory beat stimulation and reports contradictory findings across studies of cognition and mood. It highlights stimulation parameters and methodological differences as important when interpreting reported effects.
appraisal: The reviewed studies varied in stimulation methods and outcomes; contradictory results limit firm conclusions.
